title: The Good Shepherd Gathers His Scattered Flock
summary: The people are told to ask the LORD for rain rather than trust idols and diviners, whose empty comfort has left them like sheep without a shepherd. God declares his anger against the faithless shepherds and promises to care for his flock himself: from Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, and the battle bow. He will strengthen Judah, save the house of Joseph, whistle for his scattered people, and bring them home from Egypt and Assyria in a new exodus.
story: Chapter 9 announced the coming king and God's victory for his people. Chapter 10 turns to the people themselves, scattered and misled, and to their leaders, the shepherds. It develops the promise at the end of chapter 9 that God would save his people as his flock (9:16), and it widens the circle to include the northern tribes, called here Joseph and Ephraim, who had been exiled by Assyria nearly two centuries before Zechariah. The shepherd theme will dominate chapter 11, where the relationship between God, the shepherds, and the flock breaks down.
historical:
The northern kingdom of Israel, often called Ephraim or the house of Joseph after its leading tribes, fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and many of its people were deported (2 Kings 17:5-6). The southern kingdom of Judah fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. In the Persian period Jews lived not only in Judah and Babylonia but also in Egypt, where a Jewish military colony at Elephantine on the Nile is well documented in the fifth century BC. The promise to bring people back from Egypt and Assyria therefore spoke to a real dispersion in many lands. By Zechariah's day Assyria had not existed as an empire for about a century, and Egypt was under Persian rule, so the names likely function as traditional labels for the lands of exile and oppression, drawn from older prophecy (Isaiah 11:11-16; Hosea 11:11). Some scholars who date these chapters to the Greek period read Assyria and Egypt as code for the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms that succeeded Alexander, but that reading depends on the later date.

Gilead and Lebanon (verse 10) were regions east of the Jordan and north of Galilee that had once belonged to Israel's territory. The promise that there will be no room for all the returnees reverses the thin population of post-exilic Judah.
cultural:
In a land without rivers for irrigation, life depended on the rains. The early rains in autumn softened the ground for plowing and sowing, and the later or spring rains in March and April filled out the grain before harvest; the word in verse 1 refers to these spring rains. Canaanite religion credited Baal, the storm god, with the rain, and Israel was repeatedly tempted to seek fertility from him. Zechariah reminds the people that the LORD makes the storm clouds.

The household idols of verse 2 (Hebrew teraphim) were small images kept in homes and used in divination, as Rachel's stolen idols were (Genesis 31:19). Diviners sought hidden knowledge by reading signs, and dream interpreters by reading dreams; the law forbade such practices in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-14). Across the ancient Near East kings were commonly called shepherds of their people, so the shepherds and leaders (literally male goats, the lead animals of a flock) in verse 3 are rulers. The cornerstone held a building's walls together, the tent peg held a tent up (compare Isaiah 22:23), and the battle bow was the weapon of a warrior: three images for strong and dependable leaders.
literary: The chapter is poetry, much of it spoken by God in the first person. It moves from a short exhortation (verses 1-2), to God's judgment on the shepherds and his care for the flock (verses 3-5), to an extended promise of restoration (verses 6-12). The central image shifts playfully: the flock of verse 3 becomes a royal war horse, and then mighty warriors. The restoration borrows the language of the exodus: passing through the sea, striking the waves, drying up the depths of the Nile, the scepter of Egypt departing. Repeated verbs carry the promise: I will strengthen, I will save, I will restore, I will whistle, I will gather, I will bring them back. The chapter opens and closes on God: ask the LORD in verse 1, in His name they will walk in verse 12.

outline.t: Ask the LORD for rain, not the idols
Against the shepherds; from Judah come cornerstone and tent peg
God whistles for his scattered people and brings them home

doctrines.note: Idols and diviners speak deceit and offer empty comfort, and the people who follow them wander like lost sheep. The LORD alone gives rain and life; trust in any other source misleads and harms.

God's rescue is described as a new exodus: he redeems, gathers, and brings his people through the sea. Salvation here is God's initiative from start to finish, grounded in his compassion, so that they will be as though I had not rejected them.

God refuses to leave his people without a shepherd. He judges false leaders and promises that true ones, a cornerstone and a tent peg, will come from Judah, and he gathers a divided people, Judah and Joseph, into one flock.

words.note: Raah, to shepherd, pasture, or tend. As a participle it is the ordinary word for shepherd, and throughout the ancient Near East it was used of kings. The absence of a shepherd in verse 2 and God's anger at the shepherds in verse 3 set up chapter 11 and recall Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's shepherds and promises to shepherd his sheep himself.

Pinnah, corner, and hence cornerstone. The cornerstone was the key stone at the corner where walls met, holding the structure together. It became a common image for a leader, and Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16 use the related image of a precious cornerstone.

Sharaq, to whistle or hiss. It can describe the whistle of scorn at a ruin, but here it is a shepherd's or beekeeper's call gathering his flock. Isaiah 5:26 and 7:18 use it of God summoning distant nations; here God whistles to call his own people home.

Padah, to ransom or redeem, to buy back something or someone by paying a price. It is used of the exodus from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). God says he has redeemed his people, and the gathering follows from that act.

christ: When Jesus saw the crowds, he had compassion on them because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36; Mark 6:34), a picture found here in verse 2 and earlier in Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34:5. He called himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and who has other sheep to bring into one flock (John 10:11-16). The chapter's promise that the cornerstone will come from Judah finds its New Testament fulfillment in Jesus, from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14), whom the apostles call the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:6-7), though the Greek texts quote Psalm 118 and Isaiah 28 rather than this verse. The new exodus pattern of gathering and redemption also shapes the New Testament's telling of Jesus's work: Luke describes his coming death in Jerusalem using the Greek word exodus (Luke 9:31). The links here are patterns fulfilled rather than direct predictions.
questions: The people sought comfort from idols and diviners and were left wandering. Where do people today look for guidance that leaves them lost?
God judges shepherds who fail the flock. What does this chapter say to those who lead others in any setting?
God promises to treat his people as though he had never rejected them. What does that kind of restoration mean for someone who has wandered?
